seasons.review_body: Bodies dropped on Netflix on 19 October 2023, adapted from Si Spencer's graphic novel by Paul Tomalin and produced by Sid Gentle Films. The series deploys four detectives across four Londons - 1890 (Kyle Soller as DI Hillinghead), 1941 (Shira Haas as DC Maplewood), 2023 (Amaka Okafor as DS Hasan), and 2053 (Jacob Fortune-Lloyd as DS Weissman) - each investigating the same impossible corpse. Critics approved at 81 percent from 27 reviewers; The Guardian found it more than able to sustain the ambition of its central conceit. Stephen Graham's work across the timelines was singled out as the performance that unified an otherwise segmented narrative. Audience scores at 7.3 on IMDb reflected solid engagement, with genre fans who came via Dark and Cloud Atlas most enthusiastic. The primary critical caveat was the exposition-heavy final episode, which works to collapse the four threads into a single explanation.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Bodies S01E01: "Episode 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The shock goes up to 360. The room starts compressions, stops them, starts again. **Karen Taylor** is no longer a case on a list or a name in a handoff. She is the point where procedure has to prove it can carry a life. That is the premiere’s argument in miniature: medicine here is a chain of decisions, and every link has a person attached.

Bodies opens with job titles, referrals, theatre lists, transfers, histology, hospice beds and emergency drugs. Then it asks the only question that matters. When the body fails, who owns the failure?

## The Job Title Is a Trap

**Rob Lake** arrives looking for **Mr. Hurley’s** firm, and the episode wastes no time turning that arrival into pressure. **Sister Ricks** introduces him as **Roger Hurley’s** new SPR, a line of authority that sounds tidy for about ten seconds. It gives Rob status, access and proximity to difficult decisions. It also places him directly under the light when something goes wrong.

The early Rob is built through competence language. He reports that the CA area has been excised completely and that histology is awaited. Clean information. Proper hierarchy. A doctor speaking in the vocabulary of control. The hour’s best move is to let that control curdle without changing the surface texture. Rob keeps using the right words later. He calls, explains, justifies and reaches for the right chain of command. The situation has already moved from medicine into blame.

The cricothyrotomy failure becomes the hinge. Rob wants the ENT help to have happened correctly. Instead, he is pressed over whether the referral was placed properly, then has to call ENT urgently. He admits the procedure went wrong, but tries to widen the conversation to the way blame gets assigned after an off day, a bad call, a panicked moment. The episode gives him no clean escape. It also avoids the comfort of a single villain. That is a strong first-hour instinct, because the fear in Bodies comes from proximity. Nobody is far enough from the error to feel safe.

## Lists Are Control Until Bodies Interrupt

The premiere understands that hospital drama lives or dies in administration. That sounds dry until the episode proves otherwise. **Maya** asking **Donna** to change the theatre list and put **Mrs. Collier** first is a miniature power map. Lists decide order. Order decides urgency. Urgency decides who gets seen before another body deteriorates.

Donna is the hour’s clearest procedural force. She blocks **Mrs. Bourne** in the acute ward until transfer to **Newland’s** hospice, then later moves with hard speed when **Angela Strawberry’s** sore throat crisis escalates. The writing draws a useful line through her: the same character who insists on proper transfer also orders urgent adrenaline and IV cortisone when the situation demands it. She is written as a person who knows that care can be a form, a bed or a drug given now.

That precision matters because Bodies is dense. The role callouts and medical handoffs come thick, and the episode occasionally risks turning people into job functions. Donna is the counterweight. Her scenes give the bureaucracy a pulse. She understands process as a tool, not a refuge. When she holds a line, the line has a purpose. When she breaks into emergency action, the authority feels earned because the groundwork has already been laid.

That is where the premiere starts to separate itself from a simpler hospital-pressure drama. The paperwork is not background noise. It is part of the danger. The wrong order, the wrong assumption, the wrong delay can travel through the building before anyone knows what it has cost.

## The Sore Throat Becomes a Trial

Angela Strawberry’s crisis is the premiere’s cleanest escalation. A sore throat should be small. Here it becomes the episode’s moral pressure cooker, because the danger grows faster than the system can comfortably absorb. Donna orders adrenaline and IV cortisone. Rob is pushed toward ENT. The referral question becomes a blade.

The important beat arrives when Donna tells Rob that ENT had an emergency, and that survival was not guaranteed even then. That line of reasoning complicates the blame math. It gives Rob a possible defence without making him innocent. It gives the system an explanation without making the system safe. The episode keeps those distinctions alive. Bad outcomes do not automatically prove bad doctors. Proper process does not automatically rescue anyone. Bodies plants itself in that ugly middle and stays there.

The two long silence spans in the hour’s rhythm matter here. After so much high-density procedural talk, silence becomes a violent cut. The episode is at its best when it lets a pause do what another explanation cannot. The weakness is that some transitions hit with less emotional preparation than they need. The abruptness suits the hospital, but it can leave a character beat feeling filed rather than felt.

Even then, the design is clear. The show wants the viewer inside the scramble, not outside with a neat case summary. That choice has costs. Names and functions arrive quickly, and the emotional map sometimes trails the clinical one. But the pressure works because the episode trusts procedure to carry dread. Nobody has to announce the stakes. The room does it.

## Roger Hurley’s Shadow Falls Across Every Room

Roger Hurley enters the episode as a center of gravity before he fully becomes the problem. Rob is attached to his firm. High-stakes cases orbit him. He relies on operative judgment, but the episode also places that judgment under attack. He is challenged over postoperative mortality, and later faces accusations tied to repeated mistakes.

That is smart placement for a first episode. Bodies refuses to isolate the Angela crisis from the larger institutional tremor around Hurley. It lets one failure echo against another set of questions. Rob’s individual panic, Donna’s emergency response, the theatre list, the hospice transfer and Hurley’s challenged record all belong to the same machine. Each beat asks how hospitals distribute responsibility when authority is layered and time is short.

Karen Taylor’s crash brings that structure to its bluntest image. The 360 shock is a number, almost mechanical. The starting and stopping of compressions is action stripped of decoration. Yet the episode places it near the final accusation energy, where the question shifts from what happened to whether somebody caused it. That turn is the hook. It does not need fireworks. It needs the cold suspicion that a body on a hospital bed may also be evidence.

The season work is already visible. The cricothyrotomy fallout gives Rob a professional and moral wound. Hurley’s record opens a larger question about protected authority and repeated error. The unresolved maternity-unit accountability conflict broadens the premise beyond one ward or one bad outcome. The premiere does not scatter these threads. It threads them through the same anxiety: a hospital can know exactly who holds each title and still struggle to say who is responsible.

## The Verdict

Bodies opens with a confident, abrasive procedural hour that treats hospital systems as character drama. The best scenes turn forms, transfers, referrals and emergency orders into moral choices. Rob’s panic, Donna’s control and Hurley’s contested authority give the premiere a strong engine, even when the density of names and roles crowds the emotional entry points. The first episode is sharp enough to make process feel dangerous and restrained enough to avoid easy blame. Its season work is clear too, planting the cricothyrotomy fallout, the questions around repeated errors connected to Hurley, and the unresolved maternity-unit accountability conflict. Score: 8.0.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere introduces all four timelines within a single episode, each anchored to Longharvest Lane and a naked male corpse with a bullet wound. The cross-cutting is disciplined rather than dazzling - Tomalin establishes the rules of the conceit cleanly before the series earns its right to complicate them. Each detective has a distinct register, and the production design work across four distinct period Londons is immediately impressive.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 8
episode_reviews.review_body: Bodies' finale assembles all four timelines into a single explanatory framework and delivers the structural payoff the series spent seven episodes building toward. The exposition required to close the temporal loop is the episode's weakest stretch - there is a section of the finale where the mechanics of the conceit require dialogue that functions more as explanation than drama. The audience that invested in the character work across the preceding hours will find the emotional resolution sufficient: what the loop means for each detective's individual arc is resolved with more care than the mythology required. The audience watching primarily for the puzzle mechanics will note that the solution is tidier than the build-up suggested, with some of the ambiguity the earlier episodes sustained necessarily foreclosed by the finale's explanatory commitments. The show's 74 percent Rotten Tomatoes score across the season reflects a divided critical response between those who found the conclusion satisfying and those who found it slightly deflating.
